report:
Your “no” is supported: CoQ10 is not an evidence-based treatment to improve Parkinson’s movement symptoms. The rationale was plausible—mitochondrial dysfunction/oxidative stress—and a small 2002 trial reported slower functional decline, but its own authors said confirmation was needed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12374491/). The definitive NIH-funded QE3 randomized trial in early PD found high-dose CoQ10 safe but with “no evidence of clinical benefit” (https://read.qxmd.com/read/24664227/a-randomized-clinical-trial-of-high-dosage-coenzyme-q10-in-early-parkinson-disease-no-evidence-of-benefit). Later RCT syntheses/meta-analyses likewise have not shown consistent, clinically meaningful improvement in UPDRS motor/function outcomes (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10072-016-2757-9). NCCIH summarizes CoQ10 as unproven for PD (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/coenzyme-q10).

Bottom line: don’t use CoQ10 to treat tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, gait, or balance, and don’t substitute it for levodopa/other indicated therapies. If someone still wants to try it, discuss dose, cost, quality control, and interactions—especially warfarin—with their neurologist.
